content:
Ep 9 ELEM — Writing about Topics & Texts

In this episode, we'll combine information presented previously in order to connect the skills we TEACH with the TOPICS & TEXTS students write about. By doing this, we'll get a clearer picture of how writing-INSTRUCTION and writing-PRACTICE unfold within a single unit.

To start, let's go back to what we covered in the several previous episodes. In Episode 1, we covered the need for whole-class instruction on grade-level skills—followed by time for students to apply them in their writing. In Episode 2, we broke down a mini-lesson and how it follows the gradual release—including I do, We do, and You do. In more recent episodes, we targeted Persuasive, Informative, and Narrative writing. While we've focused on WHICH SKILLS to teach, we have not spent time addressing WHAT students are writing ABOUT. That's our focus in this episode.

Ep 9 ELEM — Three Common Writing Topics

Three common writing topics are: general knowledge, core knowledge, and texts.

1. GENERAL KNOWLEDGE includes writing topics that ALL students can relate to because they're part of daily school life—like lunch, recess, or walking in the hallway. This differs from personal experiences—like vacations or family events—which vary and may not be shared by all students.

2. CORE-KNOWLEDGE writing topics come from academic subjects like science, social studies, and math. This type of writing showcases each student's content knowledge WITHIN writing.

3. And after reading TEXTS, students can write summaries, compare multiple texts, or research and synthesize information into a report.

While we've likely assigned each of these types of writing before, WHEN we use which one matters. To set students up for productive writing practice, we need to follow four key principles when planning units.

section_name: Key Principle #1 — EOU Product Is the Assessment
content:
Ep 9 ELEM — Key Principle #1: The EOU product is the assessment, not the daily writing topic.

Often, the writing students work on DURING a unit is the same piece they submit for assessment at the END. While common, this approach isn't ideal. For one reason, while students are learning and practicing each new skill during writing time, they're likely receiving LOTS of help and support—maybe from peers, but definitely from us! And if we assess that SAME writing, we don't truly know what THEY, individually, have learned as writers. We don't know how much of the final piece reflects their OWN skills versus input from a classmate or YOU.

The purpose of an END-of-unit product is to assess what students have learned DURING the unit. Meaning—students are to write about DIFFERENT topics DURING the unit, saving the END-of-unit topic for an informal assessment.

section_name: Key Principle #1 — First Grade Informative Unit Example
content:
Ep 9 ELEM — Key Principle #1: Planning a Unit Example (First Grade Informative)

Let's look at this within an example unit. Imagine I'm a first grade teacher planning an informative writing unit. Using my state's standards to identify the writing skills to teach, I settle on these 3:
1. How to name the topic
2. How to write facts about the topic
3. How to include details about the topic

After determining the skills to teach, I would jump to the end of the unit and determine what to assess. Let's assume my first-grade team and I have already planned for students to write a multi-sentence informative piece about a content-area concept we've studied—like a community helper, a type of weather, or an environment such as the desert or forest. Whatever the EOU writing topic is, remember: students will not write about it DURING the unit.

With the writing skills identified and the end product determined, it's time to plot the MLs. Knowing that most skills require multiple days of instruction, my informative unit might look like this:
– 3 MLs to teach HOW to list facts about a topic
– 2 MLs to teach HOW to include additional, smaller sensory details
– 1 ML on HOW the first thing to tell the reader is the topic you're writing about
– And 2 more MLs to REVIEW how to stretch words into complete thoughts

Let me pause to note that this approach works even if students aren't writing full sentences. The same skills can be taught and practiced through pictures and labels. Likewise, intermediate teachers can apply this framework to multi-paragraph writing. This is just one unit example—but the unit-planning process is the same across all grade levels and writing units.

section_name: EOU Product — Game Day & All-By-Yourself Writing
content:
Ep 9 ELEM — EOU Product: Game Day and Introducing the Assessment

If writing DURING the unit is PRACTICE, then the EOU product is GAME day. All of these daily writing times have prepared students to now make the shift from practice to performance.

When it's time to introduce the EOU product, use the next day's mini-lesson to explain the expectations. This includes announcing the writing topic, outlining specific requirements, reviewing recently taught skills, and updating the rubric to account for them. Then, during THAT day's writing time, students compose their pieces independently.

Now, you could interpret this to be LIKE A TESTING environment—after all, it IS a performance assessment. But I don't tend to think of it that rigidly. I more gently refer to this as "all by yourself writing day." I want to see what they can do as writers, all by themselves.

Back in my hypothetical first grade classroom, it might sound like this:
"Writers, we've learned so much about how we can write to inform someone! We learned—How to teach our reader by sharing facts about a topic. How to add small, close-up details with our 5 senses. And how to always start our writing by telling the reader what the topic is that we're going to teach them about."
"Well, today, you're going to use ALL of your new informative writing skills in one, big writing! You're going to try your best to teach someone everything you know about... the desert! You'll use the skills you've learned—listing facts, adding close-up details, and stretching it all into sentences. This is an all-by-yourself writing day, so we won't be working with our classmates. This is one of those times that writers work alone. I'm so excited to read what you write! OK, writers, NIYT"

section_name: EOU Product — Independent Writing & Multi-Day Completion
content:
Ep 9 ELEM — EOU Product: Independent Writing Time and Completion

After I tell students what they're writing about, they transition into independent Writing Time—listing facts, adding details, and then expanding those into sentences. I'm not guiding the class through this process; that was taught and practiced early, DURING the unit.

Now, while I won't walk around OFFERING help, I also won't ignore students who are completely stuck. My bigger goal is to see what each student can do on his own—what skills have been mastered, and which ones need more support.

Depending on the size of the EOU writing task, students may not finish in a single writing time—and that's okay. Simply have them continue the next day. Begin with a brief meeting to refocus on the task and key skills, then send them off to keep writing about... the desert.

This results in a complete first draft—which is exactly what students are expected to produce independently on state assessments. However, if you want students to also revise, edit, and publish their writing, you'll need to plan additional days at the end of the unit for those steps of the writing process.

section_name: Key Principle #2 — Practice with General Knowledge Topics
content:
Ep 9 ELEM — Key Principle #2: Students practice new writing skills with general knowledge topics.

With the instruction and assessment planned, now we need to determine what TOPICS the students are writing about DURING the unit.

Each day, after the mini-lesson, students write for a very specific purpose—to experiment with THAT day's ML skill. Consequently, our job is to provide writing TIME and writing TOPICS that allow them to do that. However:

– If we let them "pick a topic," some will sit there unsure of what to write.
– If we rely on personal experiences, not all students will have background knowledge to draw from.
– If writing today depends on reading comprehension or core content knowledge, some will struggle to get started.

Each of these writing scenarios comes back to the same problem—students can't practice a new WRITING skill if they lack knowledge, comprehension, or understanding of the TOPIC that they're supposed to write about.

When we ask students to try a new writing skill, we want them focused on using THAT skill, not on figuring out what details to include or if their information is accurate. If they are trying to fill in knowledge gaps on the TOPIC, then their mental energy is no longer focused on APPLYING the new writing skill. When they are juggling both complex content AND an unfamiliar writing skill, the process is slow, frustrating, and often UNproductive.

section_name: Key Principle #2 — Reducing Cognitive Load & Building Up Rigor
content:
Ep 9 ELEM — Key Principle #2: Reducing Cognitive Load and Building Up to Rigor

THEREFORE, when the difficulty and complexity of the writing skill is HIGH, we need to give them familiar topics to reduce cognitive load. If we temporarily remove the content barrier, we give students a chance to focus on mastering the writing skill first—without the added challenge of a difficult topic.

Don't misunderstand—we're not removing rigor; we're WORKING UP to it. We don't prepare for a marathon by running 10 miles on the first day—we BUILD UP to it. Similarly, as students get more comfortable with a WRITING skill and gain confidence in how to use it, then we can increase the rigor of the TOPICS that they're writing ABOUT. This includes writing about core knowledge, subject area concepts, and writing about reading.

Consequently, a key factor in ALL of the writing tasks that are given DURING the unit, is to have students write about general knowledge topics—topics all students can relate to and write about with ease. These topics are part of their everyday lives, so the students are already deeply familiar with them.
skill_title: Reducing Cognitive Load & Building Up Rigor

section_name: General Knowledge Topic Examples & Recycling Across Writing Purposes
content:
Ep 9 ELEM — Naming General Knowledge Topics and Recycling Them Across Writing Purposes

Let's more specifically name some general knowledge topics, because it's often misunderstood as simply writing about school. But "SCHOOL" is NOT a writing topic—it's a giant subject matter. I don't want ANY grade level writing about SCHOOL! That's like writing about LIFE! No, think smaller. Think about the components of a school day: Recess, Specials, Procedures. Now go even smaller. List EACH special YOUR students attend—Art, music, PE, library—each of these is a general knowledge writing topic. Students could write about individual procedures: beginning of day procedures, end of day procedures, procedures for each class job. Smaller topics for recess might be games, equipment, weather.

Each of these narrower topics is something students know a lot about—WHICH IS EXACTLY WHAT MAKES them GREAT for practicing new writing skills! These are great everyday topics that all students can relate to, giving them ALL built-in knowledge to draw from.

Additionally, we can recycle these general knowledge topics if we think of them in terms of the different writing purposes. For example:

In an informative unit, writing about lunch might include:
– Explaining the food and drink choices one makes when going through the line
– Or the procedures for how to leave the table and head to recess

In a persuasive unit, writing about lunch might include:
– Persuading the cafeteria workers to add a new menu item
– Or persuading the lunch aides to change a cafeteria rule

In a narrative unit, writing about lunch might include a problem like:
– A time you had trouble opening a lunch item
– A time you dropped or spilled something at lunch

So LUNCH? This isn't merely a general knowledge topic to write about ONCE. It's a topic we can revisit throughout the year—each time narrowing the focus to fit the UNIT and skills we're teaching and practicing.

section_name: Key Principle #3 — Each Day Requires 3 Writing Topics
content:
Ep 9 ELEM — Key Principle #3: Each day of instruction requires 3 writing "topics."

As we continue thinking about writing topics, let's identify how many are needed throughout a unit. Now, notice the quotes around the word "topics." This is much more manageable than it seems.

In Episode 2, I walked through the 4-steps of a mini lesson and identified the components of the gradual release.
– We know that the teacher models the skill all by herself during the I DO. So that will require a "topic."
– Then, in the same 15 min ML, you invite students to help you execute the same skill a second time. This requires a second "topic."
– The lesson ends when you announce the YOU DO task—or what students will do during WT to practice this new skill. This requires a third "topic."

So, for each day's ML, we need 3 "topics"—we need to provide 3 OPPORTUNITIES for students to EXPERIENCE the new writing skill.

section_name: Unit Example — Selecting PE Game Topics for I Do, We Do, You Do
content:
Ep 9 ELEM — Building the Informative Unit: Selecting Topics for I Do, We Do, You Do

Let's continue building that informative writing unit for first grade. The first day of this unit, I will teach students that informative writing includes writing facts about a topic. That means I need 1 topic to model making a list of facts in the I DO. I'll need a second topic to model making a list of facts in the WE DO. And a third topic for students to make a list of facts in their YOU DO.

When considering what these topics could be, we want to focus on general knowledge topics—those that ALL kids can relate to through shared school experiences. But I'm not picking topics randomly—in this informative writing unit, I know I want to emphasize the importance of exact words and facts. And lunch items and recess equipment are too generic. So I'm thinking of topics that would allow for more specialized vocabulary.

I'm thinking about specials like art, music, and PE. And I recall students have been talking about games they've learned in PE—like Tic Tac Toe Relay, Red light green light, Monster Ball, Blob tag, Fleas Off the Parachute. Each game has different equipment, steps, players, positions, and scoring. These would be great GENERAL knowledge topics to use for practicing the new INFORMATIVE writing skills I'm teaching.

To determine which topics I use in the ML and the ones THEY use in WT, always choose the more difficult one for yourself. Applying this to PE games, I'll begin with Red light, green light for the I DO—it's more abstract, there's no equipment and it's mostly just about rules and objectives. Then, in the WE DO, the students help me apply the skill using a topic that is easier to work with. I'll use Tic Tac Toe Relay—it has some equipment and a little more action. And ALWAYS save the most fun and most concrete topics for the YOU DO in order to increase their motivation to apply this skill on their own. In that case, I'd give them Monster Ball, Blob tag, and Fleas Off the Parachute.
skill_title: Selecting PE Game Topics for I Do, We Do, You Do

section_name: Key Principle #4 — You-Do Task Mirrors the I-Do Model
content:
Ep 9 ELEM — Key Principle #4: The You-Do task always mirrors the I-Do model.

Now I can anticipate that some may be thinking: "I can barely get kids to turn in the one writing due at the end of the unit! How will they ever do more than one?" Let's address this by looking at key principle #4: The You-Do task always mirrors the I-Do model.

We've spent this whole episode talking about writing TOPICS. Now let's shift to writing TASKS. This is about what students are actually DOING with the topic during writing time—what they're writing down and HOW MUCH they're writing.

The answer is always the same—they write as much as you wrote. Whatever you did in the mini-lesson model is what the students will do during writing time. Their task is parallel to yours. The only thing that changes is the TOPIC. That's the WHOLE MEANING of gradual release. We have to release them... to do... what we did.

Consequently, if I just made a list of facts—then that's all the students will do during WT. This is why I like to have SEVERAL you-do TOPICS ready to go. Not only can you give students choice, but more importantly, if a student gets "done" with one topic, he can practice the skill AGAIN with another topic. The purpose of writing time isn't to DO the task—it's to practice a new skill as much as possible!
skill_title: You-Do Task Mirrors the I-Do Model

section_name: Unit Example — Days 2 and 3 Building on Same Topics
content:
Ep 9 ELEM — Building the Informative Unit: Days 2 and 3 with Cumulative Topics

Let's now go back to our first grade informative writing unit one last time and build out the YOU DO tasks that will follow each day's ML.

On day two, I'll remind students that informative writing is about facts and focus on breaking down the topic into even smaller parts. In my I do, I'll revisit the fact list I made yesterday about Red Light/Green Light. I'll reread it, and note the general ideas I listed previously and think aloud about specific steps to the game and add them. In the We Do, I'll guide them to help me do the same thing with the Tic Tac Toe Relay list. Then, during the You Do, students will reread their own lists from the previous day and look for places to add more specifics about the steps or procedures of the game.

Notice I still had three topics for the second day of this unit. They are just the same three topics from Day 1.

On day three, I'll layer in the importance of action verbs in informative writing. In my I do, I'll revisit my on-going Red light/green light list and show how to connect some action verbs to the facts I'd previously listed. I'll guide them to help me do the same in the Tic Tac Toe Relay list. And then they will add action verbs to their lists, too.

Each day of the unit is like learning a new step in a dance—after teaching a little bit about a skill, the teacher gives students TIME and TOPICS to practice that skill. Teach, model, guide, release. This occurs each day of the writing unit.
skill_title: Days 2 and 3 Building on Same Topics

content:
Ep 9 ELEM — Wrap-Up and Key Takeaway

This cumulative writing practice DURING the unit prepares students to bring all the skills together within an EOU writing product—which is often about a core knowledge concept or response to text. By the time we get to this new and more complex topic at the END of the unit, students have grown in their confidence and competence with these skills because of the practice DURING the unit. They are better prepared to tackle this task more independently.

Now, there IS more to planning writing units and we'll continue the conversation in Episode 10. But for now, let me wrap up this video with the most important takeaway:

Writing units provide direct instruction on grade-level skills, followed by in-class writing time and general-knowledge topics to practice EACH one, all BEFORE asking students to apply them cumulatively within a NEW product at the end of the unit.

By honoring these key principles when planning and delivering writing instruction, we take the next step toward building better writers.
